::: {.lead}
Night Owl Games plans a new level for *Rooftop Rescue*: "Storm Night", in
which Nour and Pasha the cat cross the roofs in a thunderstorm. Salma, the
producer, needs a **media package** in two workshop sessions: a storyboard,
a sound set, a 30-second promo clip and a credits file. In this course you
learned each part alone: storyboards (lectures 9–12), sound and music
(lectures 13–18), video (lectures 19–22) and intellectual property
(lectures 23–26). In this workshop you make **all of them for one brief**, in a small
production team or alone, role by role. Every section ends with a short
task, and the team activity describes the whole workshop.
:::

## Key terms

{{< glossary media-package production-brief production-role production-schedule handoff naming-convention production-log quality-review storyboard promo-clip credits-file >}}

## 27.1 The brief and the package

A production starts with a **brief** that everyone can check (@fig-package).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 27.1 — Production brief and media package"}
A **production brief** says what to make, for whom, in which format and
length, and by when. The **media package** of this workshop:

- a **storyboard** of 6 panels with a shot list (C1);
- a **sound set**: 3 sound effects and 1 seamless music loop (C2);
- a **promo clip** of 30 s, 16:9, 1920 × 1080, with music (C3);
- a **credits file** with TASL for every asset that is not your own (D1);
- a **quality review** against the brief (B2).
:::

![The media package for "Storm Night".](images/package.png){#fig-package width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 27.1 — Salma's brief"}
1. *For whom:* players of *Rooftop Rescue* on phones and PCs.
2. *Mood:* dark blue night, rain, lightning; the music is tense but not
   scary.
3. *Formats:* panels as PNG; sounds as 48 kHz WAV; the promo as MP4 16:9,
   peaks at −1 dB or lower.
4. *Deadline:* the end of the second session; the presentation in lecture
   28.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Starting to produce before reading the brief together. Ten minutes on the
brief saves an hour of work in the wrong format.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Read the brief"}
Write the brief of your own package in five lines: what, for whom, mood,
formats, deadline. (Use "Storm Night" or a level of your own game idea.)

*Your result:* a five-line brief.
:::

## 27.2 Roles, schedule and handoffs

A small team splits the work into **roles** and plans the **handoffs**
(@fig-roles, @fig-pipeline).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 27.2 — Roles and schedule"}
- **Producer:** brief, schedule, folder, names, credits file.
- **Storyboard artist:** panels, shot list, art style.
- **Sound designer:** effects, music loop, final mix.
- **Video editor:** capture, cut, titles, export.

A **production schedule** puts the tasks in order, so that each task gets
its input in time. A **handoff** is the moment finished work passes to the
next role, for example the shot list to the editor before the capture.
:::

![Four production roles.](images/roles.png){#fig-roles width=94%}

![The handoffs.](images/pipeline.png){#fig-pipeline width=94%}

![A schedule for two sessions.](images/schedule.png){#fig-schedule width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 27.2 — A late shot list"}
1. The editor wants to capture gameplay in the first half of session 1, but
   the storyboard is not finished.
2. Salma moves the capture to the second half; the editor sets up the
   project first.
3. The music loop must be ready before the cut, and the credits before the
   export (@fig-schedule).
:::

{{< sim file="sims/production-planner.html" poster="sims/production-planner.png" title="Production Planner: two sessions, eight tasks" height="640" >}}

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Everyone starting with "their" task at the same time. Tasks that need
another task's result must wait for the handoff, or the work is done twice.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Plan the sessions"}
In **Production Planner**, remove all conflicts. Write your own schedule
for the package: role, task, slot.

*Your result:* a schedule without conflicts.
:::

## 27.3 Files, names and the production log

A shared folder only works with clear rules (@fig-naming).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 27.3 — Working with files"}
- One **folder** with numbered subfolders (brief, storyboard, audio, video,
  credits, review).
- A **naming convention**: `level_type_name_version`, for example
  `storm_sfx_thunder_v02.wav`; no spaces; versions, never "final_final2".
- **One owner per file:** the editor owns the edit; the others send notes.
- A **production log**: date, who, what was made, which decision, which
  problem was solved.
:::

![One folder, one naming rule.](images/naming.png){#fig-naming width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 27.3 — The lost changes"}
1. The sound designer and the editor both open the promo project and save
   their changes; the editor's cut is overwritten.
2. New rule: only the editor saves the edit; the sound designer exports
   `storm_music_loop_v03.wav` into `03_audio`.
3. The log says: "12:40, Yara, music loop v03, shortened to 8 bars; Tariq
   imports v03."
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Keeping assets only on one person's laptop. If that person is absent, the
package is missing. Everything goes into the shared folder.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Folder and log"}
Create the folder structure of @fig-naming (on your computer or in the
cloud) and write the first three lines of your production log.

*Your result:* a folder and three log lines.
:::

## 27.4 Checking the package against the brief

Before the presentation, the team checks every part against the brief.

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 27.4 — Quality review against the brief"}
For each item of the brief, write the **brief value** and the **measured
value**: panel count, clip length and shape, the loudest peak, the loop,
the credits. Mark each one **pass** or **fail**, then fix the fails and
check again. Lecture 28 adds the quality criteria for the presentation.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Example 27.4 — Version 1 of the package"}
1. The promo is 41 s (brief: 30 s) and 9:16 (brief: 16:9): fail, fail.
2. The loudest peak is 0 dB (clipping): fail. Two sounds are missing in
   the credits: fail.
3. Fixes: cut the slow intro shot, export with the 16:9 preset, lower the
   master, add two TASL lines. Version 2 passes.
:::

{{< sim file="sims/package-checker.html" poster="sims/package-checker.png" title="Package Checker: does it meet the brief?" height="700" >}}

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Checking the package only by watching it once. Measure: the length, the
shape and the peaks are numbers.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Check version 1"}
In **Package Checker**, mark and fix version 1. Then write the check table
for your own package.

*Your result:* a check table with brief, measured, pass or fail.
:::

## Team activity: the Storm Night package

::: {.callout-note title="Team activity · The Storm Night package (two workshop sessions)"}
**Team:** three or four students.

**Roles:** producer, storyboard artist, sound designer, video editor (in a
team of three, the producer also edits the credits and the review).

**Product:** one media package to the brief of section 27.1: the
storyboard, the sound set, the 30-second promo clip, the credits file and
the quality review, in one shared folder with the naming rule.

**Process:** a schedule with handoffs (section 27.2), one owner per file,
a shared production log, and a quality review at the end of session 2.

**Presentation:** six minutes in lecture 28; every member presents the part
of their own role.

**Individual alternative.** A student who works alone makes the same
package with a smaller scope (4 panels, 2 sound effects, a 20-second promo)
and takes every role in turn, in the order of the handoffs. The student
keeps a **production log** for each role (date, task, decision) and
presents the package alone in lecture 28.
:::

## Case study: Workshop Day

During the workshop, six problems come up: a storyboard that is not ready
for the capture, files called "final" and "final2", two people editing the
same project, a music loop that clicks, a promo exported in 9:16, and a
student who works alone. The Game challenge of the interactive lesson uses
these problems. In the mini-game below you choose what the team, or the
student, should do.

## Further reading

Chandler, *The Game Production Toolbox* (2020), the chapters on roles,
schedules and communication. Hight and Novak, *Game Development
Essentials: Game Project Management* (2007), Chapter 5.

## Exercises

1. What does a production brief say?
2. Name the five parts of the media package of this workshop.
3. Name the four roles and one task of each.
4. What is a handoff? Give an example.
5. Why must the credits file be ready before the export?
6. Write a file name for the second version of a rain sound effect of the
   level "storm".
7. Why one owner per file?
8. What goes into a production log?
9. Which values of the promo clip can you measure in the check?
10. What does a student who works alone do in this workshop?

## Answers to the exercises

::: {.answers}
1. What to make, for whom, in which format and length, and by when.
2. Storyboard, sound set, promo clip, credits file, quality review.
3. Producer (schedule), storyboard artist (panels), sound designer (music
   loop), video editor (cut).
4. Finished work passing to the next role; for example the shot list to the
   editor before the capture.
5. The credits must be complete and allowed before the package is
   published.
6. `storm_sfx_rain_v02.wav`.
7. So that nobody overwrites another person's changes.
8. Date, who, what was made, which decision, which problem was solved.
9. The length, the shape (aspect ratio and size), the loudest peak.
10. Makes a smaller package, takes every role in turn, and keeps a
    production log.
:::
